lesson.title: BBR: Congestion Control Without Waiting to Lose a Packet
lesson.summary: TCP BBR, developed at Google, breaks from the loss-based tradition of Reno and CUBIC by continuously modeling the network's bottleneck bandwidth and minimum round trip time and pacing traffic to match, rather than reacting after packets are already lost.
lesson.body:
Every algorithm covered so far, slow start's exponential ramp, congestion avoidance's linear climb, Reno's AIMD, and CUBIC's cubic curve, shares one underlying assumption: the way to find out how much the network can carry is to keep increasing the sending rate until packets start getting dropped, then back off. This is loss-based congestion control, and it has a structural side effect known as bufferbloat. Routers along a path typically have queues to absorb short bursts, and a loss-based sender, by design, keeps pushing until those queues are completely full and start dropping packets. That means a loss-based connection routinely operates with a nearly full router queue sitting in its path, adding real, measurable queuing delay to every packet, even though the link itself is not actually short on capacity, only on buffer space.

BBR, short for Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip propagation time, takes a fundamentally different approach, and represents a genuine departure from the loss-based lineage rather than a refinement of it. Instead of inferring capacity from when packets start disappearing, BBR builds an explicit model of the path: it continuously measures the maximum delivery rate it has observed, an estimate of the bottleneck link's bandwidth, and separately tracks the minimum RTT it has observed, an estimate of the path's propagation delay with an empty queue. With both a bandwidth estimate and a base RTT estimate in hand, BBR computes the bandwidth-delay product, the ideal amount of data that should be in flight to fully use the link without needlessly filling its queue, and paces its sending rate to match that estimate directly, rather than growing a window until something breaks.

Because link conditions change over time, BBR cannot simply compute these estimates once and stop. It cycles through operating phases to keep its model current. A STARTUP phase resembles slow start, ramping up quickly to find the bottleneck's bandwidth. A DRAIN phase follows, briefly slowing down to clear out any queue that built up during the aggressive startup probing. The steady state is PROBE_BW, where BBR paces near its current bandwidth estimate but periodically raises its rate slightly to check whether more bandwidth has become available, for example because a competing flow ended. Periodically, a PROBE_RTT phase deliberately reduces the amount of data in flight for a short interval, allowing any accumulated queue to drain so that BBR can take a fresh, accurate measurement of the true minimum RTT, since that measurement would be distorted if it were taken while a queue was sitting full.

The practical consequence is that a BBR connection, in principle, can achieve throughput comparable to loss-based algorithms while inducing much less queuing delay, since it never intentionally fills the bottleneck queue to capacity as part of its normal operation. This matters most on links with real bottleneck buffers and on paths shared with latency-sensitive traffic, where a loss-based flow's habit of filling every available buffer can add tens or hundreds of milliseconds of delay to everyone else's packets. BBR has been deployed by Google, including on YouTube traffic and within Google's own infrastructure, and is available as a selectable congestion control module on Linux. It does not eliminate packet loss entirely, and its coexistence with loss-based flows like CUBIC on shared links has been an active area of engineering and research, but its core idea, model the path directly instead of discovering its limits by breaking them, marks a real shift in how congestion control can be designed, one that does not depend on the retransmission machinery covered in the next few chapters to function, even though that machinery still exists underneath as a safety net.
